description: We're University of Guelph students who are competing in-person for this hackathon!
summary: Spectral Blink allows anyone to watch the infrared sky change with NASA's SPHEREx. In this project, you can enter either any sky position or a name, where it then pulls every SPHEREx exposure of that patch from NASA/IRSA, aligns them, and plays the sky surveys as a smooth blink animation. You can see: moving things visibly jump (allowing for easy identification of moving objects), changing things visibly pulse (aiding in the identification of stars). Given the fact that SPHEREx sees 102 infrared colours, it: measures the spectrum (allowing for measuring the brightness of that spot), shows where molecules are (aiding in the identification of specific celestial bodies), and more! So overall, this is a public-facing local web tool that displays images of the sky from SPHEREx, allows anyone to see how the sky changes over time, displays not only a series of images to make it easy to spot moving objects, but goes above and beyond to provide various details to aid in exact identification with all different kinds of data made available about such objects. This project is highly impactful as it uses all possible tools to assist in celestial object identification, being innovative through its comprehensiveness. It follows all discussed ideas in the challenge, additionally covering all nice-to-haves. This project is accessible for anyone (including both beginners and researchers).
details:
What does it do, and how does it work?

Spectral Blink lets anyone watch the infrared sky change with NASA’s SPHEREx. You enter a sky position (such as 269.45, 4.69 or 08h55m10.8s -7d14m42s) or an object name (such as WISE 0855). The app pulls every SPHEREx exposure of that patch from NASA/IRSA, aligns them, and plays the surveys as a smooth blink animation. Thus:

  • Moving things jump (nearby stars, brown dwarfs and asteroids shift position between surveys which make them easy to spot)
  • Changing things pulse (variable stars brighten and fade, making them stand out from steady ones

Given that SPHEREx sees 102 infrared colors from 0.75 to 5 microns...

  • Clicking any source plots its spectrum (its brightness at every color).

This project includes a molecule lens, which...

  • Highlights absorption from compounds (ex. methane, water, carbon dioxide and carbon monoxide)
  • This reveals what an object is made of (which is useful for determining ones such as brown dwarfs)

A Gaia overlay shows known stars at their positions on each survey date, so...

  • It flags bright sources Gaia can’t see as ones of great interest to look at

Our Python back-end queries IRSA, downloads small image cutouts, reprojects them onto a common sky grid, masks bad pixels and combines exposures with inverse-variance weighting. It reads each pixel’s wavelength from the SPHEREx WCS-WAVE table. The browser receives frames as a stream.

What benefits does it have?

  • Extremely accessible way to explore outer space and to identify new celestial objects
  • Accessible for all types of people: beginners can use simple presets, plain-language labels and keyboard shortcuts with this project whilst researchers can use spectra, brightness measurements and Gaia comparisons to analyze data
  • It’s open source!

What is the intended impact of the project?

Spectral Blink aims to make SphereX's data accessible for all people.

  • For students and amateur astronomers, it lowers the barrier of knowledge necessary. Anyone can type in a name to watch a nearby star jump across the sky, being a great tool to see how more experienced astronomers can identify these objects.
  • For researchers, it streamlines the object identification process. Spectra, brightness changes, and Gaia comparisons exist so they can quickly decide which objects deserve more analysis.

Ultimately, we want to show that NASA data can become much more valuable when more people can actually use it without any knowledge required.

What tools, languages, hardware or software did you use?

  • Data: NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA) for SPHEREx spectral images; ESA Gaia DR3 for star positions and motions; CDS Sesame/SIMBAD for resolving object names.
  • Backend: Python 3.12, FastAPI, Uvicorn, httpx, NumPy, SciPy, Astropy and reproject.
  • Front-end: TypeScript, React 19, Vite, Tailwind CSS 4, Zustand, Recharts, Radix UI and Motion, HTML.
  • Deployment: Docker.
  • Hardware: Only a computer/laptop with internet connection is required!

How is it creative?

  • It reinvents a celestial object discovery method: Pluto was found by flipping between photographs of the same sky and watching for a dot that moved! So, we wanted to greatly expand on that idea as much as possible - with a grand amount of data - to create an extremely comprehensive and useful tool.
  • It makes difference visible. Subtracting one survey from another cancels steady stars, meaning only moving objects and variables are left to be seen.
  • We also use shift-and-stack processes: By lining up frames along an object’s motion, it reveals things too faint to see in a single survey, such as WISE 0855.
  • It even makes molecules visible as an image. The molecule lens compares light inside and outside a molecular band, so ordinary stars vanish whilst methane-rich brown dwarfs glow!

What factors did your team consider?

  • Accessibility: We wanted both beginners and researchers to find great use of this project, as we find accessibility to be extremely important.
  • Data quality: Raw SPHEREx exposures contain bad pixels, saturated stars and contamination, so we ensured great data quality by masking unusable pixels using the mission’s flag bits, combining exposures with inverse-variance weighting, and using a PSF-halo method to measure the brightness of saturated stars.
  • Motion across the sky: Nearby stars move noticeably in space coordinates, so catalogue positions are moved to the date of each survey (ex. Barnard’s Star has moved about 4.5′ since J2000).
  • Staying useful over time: SPHEREx releases new data every week, so a new collection can be added with one setting without changing the code.
  • Easy to run: The project is open source and runs locally with Docker, so setup doesn’t depend on each person’s Python or Node versions.
